name: Chloe Petrov

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for talking with me. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, parties or government. Everything you say stays confidential, so you can tell me what you'd say in public and what you really think. Tell me about a normal week at university so far.

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm on a marketing and communications degree, so my week is a mix of lectures on consumer behaviour and group projects where everyone argues about fonts. I share a terraced house with four people I met through a student group chat. Friday and Saturday nights and Sunday lunch I'm a waitress at a bistro, and I film little videos of the specials for their social accounts.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: How do you use AI in all that?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: Constantly. I use it to draft captions, brainstorm project ideas and clean up my essay plans. The bistro owner doesn't know it's partly AI, and honestly the videos do better when I use it to test three headlines before I post.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. That one is called AI Plateau. If this happened, what would you say about it at university, at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's useful, but hyped. I use it daily and it saves me time, but it doesn't change the world. I'd say it's a good assistant, so people should try it and stop arguing about it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I'd feel pretty fine about AI but not about money. Rent in the house is high, tips are unreliable and my loan keeps going up. If the bistro had a quiet winter, I'd be in trouble. My average grades mean no scholarship backup.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep going: lectures, the bistro, and posting videos. I'd try to turn the videos into a small paid thing, maybe doing social posts for two or three other local cafés for a little money. I'd save a bit each month, and look for a marketing internship for the summer.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Alright, honestly. A bit tight on money, but not scared.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would a quiet winter at the bistro mean for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Maybe sixty pounds less a week, which is about my share of the food bill. I'd get a second job, probably in a bar or a shop, and I'd cut my train home. My housemates would say I could borrow, but I hate owing people.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How much do you earn from the videos?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Nothing yet, just free meals. But the owner said she'd pay me if the numbers keep going up. That's my plan, to turn the thing I like doing into the thing that pays.

say: I'd say AI is a **good assistant**, so people should try it and stop arguing.
I'd say my generation needs **real work experience**.
think: I'm fine about AI but not about **money**, with high rent and unreliable tips.
My average grades mean **no backup** if work dries up.
do: Keep the **bistro shifts** and post videos every week.
Pitch **two or three cafés** for small paid social media jobs.
feel: **Alright**, a bit tight on money but not scared.
S0.quote: I'd get a second job, probably in a bar or a shop, and I'd cut my train home.
fieldNote: Chloe is **comfortable with AI**, and her only unease is rent and tips.
Plans to monetise her videos, a typical adaptive move.
Dislikes owing housemates, which limits her safety net.

steps.text: Keep the bistro shifts on Friday, Saturday and Sunday
Pitch two cafés for paid social media posts
Save fifteen pounds a week from tips
Use AI to test three captions before each post

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust. That one is called Steady Disruption. If this happened, what would you say about it at university, at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's the beginning of a big change, and marketing will be one of the first areas. I'd tell people to learn it now, because employers will expect it. I'd also say the real skill is taste, knowing what's good.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd think my degree might lose value fast, because writing, planning and campaigns are on the list for AI. Entry-level marketing jobs are basically captions, reports and emails. But I'm already ahead of most of my course on AI, so I'd feel I have a head start.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd build a portfolio of real campaigns for small businesses using AI, and show how much better they did. I'd take a short course in data and analytics. I'd move from waitressing to a part-time marketing job at a local firm, even if it pays less, to get the title on my CV.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Excited and a bit uneasy. It's like a game that keeps changing the rules.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What do you mean by taste?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Knowing what looks right for a brand. AI makes ten captions, but someone has to choose the one that sounds like the café and not like a robot. I think that's still a person, at least for a while.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What if everyone in your course gets good at AI too?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Then it stops being an edge, and I'll need something else. Probably real relationships, like knowing the owners and being the one they call. A portfolio and a phone number beat a skill on a CV.

say: I'd say employers will **expect AI skills**, so learn it now.
I'd say the real skill is **taste**.
think: Entry-level marketing jobs are **captions, reports and emails**, which AI takes first.
I'm already ahead of my course, giving me a **head start**.
do: Build a **portfolio** of real campaigns for small businesses.
Take a short **data and analytics** course and aim for a marketing job.
feel: **Excited** and a bit uneasy, like a game with changing rules.
S1.quote: AI makes ten captions, but someone has to choose the one that sounds like the café and not like a robot.
fieldNote: Chloe sees her edge as **taste plus relationships**.
Aware that AI skill won't stay a special advantage.
Willing to take a lower-paid marketing job to get the title.

steps.text: Make a portfolio of three real campaigns for local cafés
Take a short online data and analytics course
Apply for a part-time marketing job at a local firm
Test AI tools on every caption and report

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. That one is called AGI by 2028. If this happened, what would you say about it at university, at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's insane, and nobody is ready. Two years is nothing. I'd say it online but I'd also say, let's make use of it, because freaking out doesn't pay rent.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd think my degree might not matter, but I'm not the only one. By 2028 I'd be in my second year and the entry jobs I want would be gone. I'd look at what a person can still do better: being in the room, making people feel looked after. And the bistro is that, at least until the robots arrive in 2031.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd use AI to start a tiny business straight away, probably social content and customer replies for small shops. I'd work more shifts at the bistro, and I'd ask my parents if I can come home on weekends to save rent. I'd talk to the university about switching to something with a physical job at the end.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Dizzy and wired. I'd be too busy to be scared, which is probably how I cope.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: With only 2 years, what would you decide about your degree?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep it for now, because it gives me student prices and time. But I wouldn't go into debt for a third year. If I can cover my costs from clients by the end of the first year, I'd probably leave.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How would you feel about telling your parents?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Awkward. They paid for my driving lessons and think I've got a safe plan. I'd say, I'm not giving up, I'm changing the plan, and show them a list of clients. I think that would calm them down.

say: I'd say it's **insane** but freaking out doesn't pay rent.
I'd say let's **make use** of it while everyone else is still panicking.
think: The **entry jobs** I want would be gone by my second year.
A person in the room, like at the **bistro**, still has value until 2031.
do: Start a **tiny AI business** for small shops with social content and replies.
Work more shifts and ask my parents about **weekend rent** savings.
feel: **Dizzy and wired**, too busy to be scared.
fieldNote: Chloe responds to shock with **action**, and her coping is staying busy.
Treats the degree as a temporary cover for time and prices.
Plans to show her parents a client list to reassure them.

steps.text: Sign two or three small shops for AI social content
Use AI to answer customers for those shops
Save rent by staying with my parents on weekends
Show my parents a client list and new plan

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. That one is called AGI by 2031. If this happened, what would you say about it at university, at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's something we have to get ready for, and five years is enough to get ahead if you start now. I'd say I'm lucky to be young, and I'd tell friends who aren't using AI to start.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd think I'm in a good spot compared to most people on my course. I'd graduate in 2029 with a portfolio and two years of paid clients, and then I'd have two years to establish myself. It would be tight, but I'd handle it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd work in marketing for a couple of years, ideally at an agency that does AI-heavy campaigns. I'd also freelance on the side and build a savings pot of a few thousand. I'd learn enough about data to sit in the room where decisions are made, since decisions are the last things to go.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Hopeful. Pretty tense around the edges, but hopeful.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What changes in the first year, while you can see it coming?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd stop doing the low-value tasks, like basic captions, for free. I'd focus on clients who pay. And I'd try to find someone senior at an agency who'd let me shadow them.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How would five years compare to two?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Two means scramble. Five means build. I'd have a plan with a portfolio, savings and a few relationships, which is a very different feeling from fear.

say: I'd say five years is **enough to get ahead** if you start now.
I'd tell friends who don't use AI to **start**.
think: I'm in a **good spot** compared with most of my course.
I'd graduate in 2029 with a portfolio and **two years** left to establish myself.
do: Work at an **agency** for a couple of years and freelance on the side.
Build a **savings pot** of a few thousand and learn data.
S3.quote: Two means scramble. Five means build.
fieldNote: The longer window turns Chloe's **energy** into a plan.
Calm because skills, side income and time line up.
Wants to be near decisions, which she sees as the last thing to go.

steps.text: Stop doing free captions and chase paying clients
Build a savings pot of a few thousand
Learn data basics to sit in decision meetings
Ask a senior agency person if I can shadow them

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. That one is called AGI by 2036. If this happened, what would you say about it at university, at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is loads of time and the best thing is to enjoy it and learn. I'd say I'm more excited than worried. I'd tell my friends to take chances now, because later they'll be tied down.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd think I'm lucky and that it's going to be an interesting decade. I'd have a career, maybe a flat and a business of my own. I'd worry a little about whether everything is going to be fine for people who don't try, like my cousin who doesn't use computers much.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd finish the degree, work at an agency, start a small side company and aim to buy a flat before 2036. I'd try every new tool, because I like it. I'd save for a few years and then invest in whatever seems solid.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Pretty calm. I'd feel I have room to move and some luck.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What could still go wrong for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I could get complacent. If I think I'm ahead, I might stop learning and wake up behind. Or rent could rise so much that I can't save. Money is a bigger risk than AI.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you say to your cousin that night?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say, you don't need to be a tech person, just try one thing a week. I'd sit with him and show him a free tool and let him laugh at the weird answers. He'd be fine once he's played with it.

say: I'd say ten years is **loads of time**, so enjoy it and learn.
I'd tell friends to **take chances** now.
think: I'd be **lucky**, with a career and maybe a flat by then.
I'd worry about people who **don't try**, like my cousin.
do: Finish the degree, join an agency and start a **small side company**.
**Save** for a few years and aim to buy a flat before 2036.
feel: Pretty **calm**, with room to move and some luck.
S4.quote: I could get complacent. If I think I'm ahead, I might stop learning and wake up behind.
fieldNote: Chloe's **calm** is real, but she names complacency as her own risk.
Cares about her cousin, who doesn't use computers much.
Sees money as a bigger threat than AI.

steps.text: Finish the degree and join a marketing agency
Try a new AI tool every month to stay current
Save for a flat deposit before 2036
Run a small side company for local cafés

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The two-year one, even though I'd be busy and not panic. It's just so fast, and everyone else wouldn't be ready. What would help is cheap ways to start a business, clear advice on what skills last, and rent that doesn't swallow everything.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Only that being young and good with AI doesn't mean I'm secure. My rent is high and my tips are a gamble. A lot of my friends are one bad month from trouble.

headlineQuote: Being young and good with AI doesn't mean I'm secure.
portrait: Chloe, 18, studies **marketing and communications**, waits tables at a bistro and shares a terraced house with four people.
She uses AI every day and makes **social videos** for the bistro, hoping to turn them into paid work.
She's a pragmatic centrist who turns shocks into action and stays busy.
Money is her real worry, so mild scenarios feel uneasy even though AI itself doesn't scare her.
With five or ten years she is calm, but only because skills, side income and time line up.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028** worries her most, because it is too fast and others wouldn't be ready.
whatWouldHelp: Cheap ways to **start a business**, clear advice on lasting skills and rent that doesn't swallow everything.
